modules.title: Core Java & OOP
modules.intro: Core Java interviews test the language features you use every day and the edge cases interviewers love. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with string handling (immutability, pool, StringBuilder — the #1 opener), then exception handling (checked vs unchecked, try-with-resources), then generics and wildcards (type erasure, PECS), I/O and NIO, and reflection and annotations. It closes with the comparison canon and scenario-based questions where the features combine.

modules.title: Java OOP & SOLID
modules.intro: Java OOP interview questions are the single most common opener in any backend interview, from junior to staff. This module is organized as an elevation arc so a learner reads top-to-bottom and feels the level rise. T0 Fundamentals grounds you in what OOP is and why it exists as a response to procedural programming's failures, then walks the four pillars. T1 Core Mechanics covers the daily building blocks - this/super, constructor chaining, overloading vs overriding, static. T2 Internet-Famous is the canon nearly every interview asks: SOLID (the #1 most-asked design-principle set), abstract class vs interface, composition vs inheritance, cohesion and coupling, the Law of Demeter, and the equals/hashCode contract. T3 Applied Patterns moves to code you actually ship - default/static interface methods, the diamond problem, association/aggregation/composition, enums, immutability. T4 Production & Edge Cases separates a working developer from someone who's shipped: shallow vs deep copy, marker interfaces, SerialVersionUID, inner classes, anonymous vs lambda, the Object class methods. Every answer comes with a short code snippet, the trade-off the interviewer is listening for, and the follow-up they are likely to ask next.

modules.title: Java Collections & Algorithms
modules.intro: Java Collections interview questions test how well you understand the framework you reach for every day. This module is organized as an elevation arc so a learner reads top-to-bottom and feels the level rise. It opens with the framework itself — what the Java Collections Framework is, why it replaced Vector and Hashtable, and the Set/List/Queue/Map interface hierarchy you program to — then the collection internals (HashMap buckets, collision handling, iterator semantics, ArrayDeque vs the legacy Stack). Next comes the algorithmic foundation: Big-O and amortized complexity (the language every later answer is written in), then sorting and searching (TimSort, binary search, Comparator chains), then trees and graphs (BST, traversal, BFS/DFS, Dijkstra). From there the arc moves to the internet-famous comparison canon — ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap, Stack vs Queue — the questions nearly every backend interview asks. Applied patterns follow: sliding window, two pointers, fast-slow, top-K, backtracking. Then scenario-based coding problems (reverse a linked list, LRU cache, two sum, anagrams) where the patterns meet real interview questions. The module closes with dynamic programming — optimal substructure, memoization vs tabulation, knapsack — the advanced tier that separates candidates who can recognize and structure a DP recurrence from those who can only solve the easy ones. Each answer leads with the structural insight, drops into the implementation detail a senior interviewer probes, and names the follow-up you'll get next.

modules.title: Java Streams, Lambdas & Modern Java
modules.intro: Streams and modern Java features interviews test whether you use the functional style fluently. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with lambdas and functional interfaces (the foundation — SAM, method references), then the Streams API (the centerpiece — lazy, short-circuiting, collectors), then Optional (the null-handling companion). From there it moves through Java version features (9-11, 14-17, 21) in release order so a learner sees the language evolve. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Java Concurrency & Multithreading
modules.intro: Java concurrency is the most-asked advanced Java topic and the one where depth most clearly separates candidates. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with the Java Memory Model (happens-before, visibility — the foundation everything else rests on), then threads and their lifecycle, then synchronization and locks (the primitives). Concurrent collections and thread pools follow at the core-mechanics tier, then CompletableFuture (the async composition most code uses). The advanced tier covers virtual threads (the Java 21 revolution) and concurrency patterns. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: JVM Internals & Performance
modules.intro: JVM internals is the deep-Java topic where senior interviewers probe hardest. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with JVM architecture (class loading, runtime data areas, execution engine), then memory analysis (heap regions, metaspace), then garbage collection (the GC algorithms — this is where most questions land). From there it moves to the production tier — JVM tuning, profiling and debugging — and closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Spring Core & IoC
modules.intro: Spring Core interviews test whether you understand the container, not just the annotations. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with dependency injection (the central idea — IoC, the types constructor/setter/field, the BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext container), then the bean lifecycle (the hooks interviewers probe). Spring internals and custom components follow at the mechanics tier, then AOP (proxies, pointcuts, advice) and Spring events. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Spring Boot
modules.intro: Spring Boot interviews test whether you understand the auto-configuration magic, not just that it works. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with auto-configuration (the centerpiece — how @Conditional builds the context), then starters (the dependency model), then configuration management and profiles. Embedded servers and Actuator are the production tier, then testing and troubleshooting. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Spring Data, JPA & Hibernate
modules.intro: Spring Data JPA interviews test whether you understand the ORM, not just the repository interface. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with JPA fundamentals (the EntityManager, persistence context, entity states), then Hibernate internals (the session, dirty checking, cascades). Entity relationships and the Spring Data repository layer follow, then transactions (the most-asked topic — propagation, isolation). The problem tier — N+1, query optimization, caching, batch processing — is where senior interviewers land. Migrations and multi-tenancy close the advanced tier, then comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Spring Security & Identity
modules.intro: Spring Security interviews test whether you understand the filter chain, not just the annotations. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with security fundamentals (authentication vs authorization, the filter chain), then authentication and authorization (the core flows). JWT and OAuth2 — the stateless and delegated models most production apps use — follow, then SSO and SAML. Security configuration, CORS and CSRF, and testing are the applied tier. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Spring WebFlux & Reactive Programming
modules.intro: Spring WebFlux interviews test whether you understand the reactive model, not just that it's 'non-blocking'. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with reactive programming basics (the Reactive Streams contract, the push model), then Mono and Flux (the core types). Backpressure — the signature reactive problem — follows, then the WebFlux setup and R2DBC (the reactive data tier). Error handling and testing in reactive code are the applied tier. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Spring Batch & Scheduling
modules.intro: Spring Batch interviews test whether you understand batch as a pattern with its own architecture, not just a loop. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with batch fundamentals (why batch, the Job/Step model), then job and step structure, then chunk processing (the core pattern — reader/processor/writer). Item readers/writers/processors and error handling follow at the mechanics tier, then scheduling (Spring's @Scheduled and Quartz) at the applied tier. Partitioning and parallel steps close the advanced tier, then comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: SQL & Relational Databases
modules.intro: SQL database interviews test whether you can reason about query plans and transaction semantics, not just write SELECTs. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with SQL fundamentals (the relational model, the clauses), then joins and subqueries, then transactions and ACID (the most-asked topic — isolation levels, anomalies). Connection pooling, indexes, and query optimization are the performance tier — where senior interviewers probe. The advanced tier covers migrations, window functions, partitioning/sharding, replication, and backup/recovery. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: PostgreSQL
modules.intro: PostgreSQL is a single-topic module. This module covers PostgreSQL features — JSONB, CTEs, window functions, indexing (B-tree, GIN, GiST), EXPLAIN, partitioning, full-text search — organized as an elevation arc within the one topic from the fundamentals through to the advanced features that separate Postgres users from Postgres experts.

modules.title: NoSQL & MongoDB
modules.intro: NoSQL and MongoDB interviews test whether you understand the document model and when to choose it over relational. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with NoSQL fundamentals (the CAP trade-off, the four NoSQL families), then MongoDB core (the document, the collection, the BSON), then the document model (embedding vs referencing). Indexes and Elasticsearch follow at the mechanics tier, then Spring Data MongoDB at the code tier. NoSQL patterns close the applied tier, then comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Redis & Caching
modules.intro: Redis and caching interviews test whether you understand the cache as a system with its own failure modes. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with Redis data structures (the primitives — strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets), then caching strategies (cache-aside, read-through, write-through) and patterns. Cache invalidation — the hardest problem — follows, then Redis persistence and the Spring Data Redis code tier. Caffeine (the in-process cache), distributed caching, and Redis advanced features (Lua, pub/sub, streams) are the advanced tier. It closes with performance optimization, comparisons, and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: REST API & Spring MVC
modules.intro: REST API interviews are the bread-and-butter backend surface. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with REST fundamentals (what REST is, the constraints, Richardson maturity), then request/response handling and Spring MVC controllers (the code tier). REST clients (RestClient, WebClient, Feign) follow, then the design tier — error handling, versioning, API design, HATEOAS, OpenAPI. HTTP caching closes the production tier, then comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: GraphQL with Spring
modules.intro: GraphQL is a single-topic module. This module covers GraphQL fundamentals — schema, queries, mutations, subscriptions, resolvers, N+1, DataLoader — organized as an elevation arc within the one topic so a learner reads top-to-bottom from 'what is GraphQL' through to production concerns.

modules.title: gRPC for Java Services
modules.intro: gRPC is a single-topic module. This module covers gRPC fundamentals — protocol buffers, the four service types, streaming, deadlines, interceptors, error handling — organized as an elevation arc within the one topic from 'what is gRPC and why vs REST' through to production patterns.

modules.title: Microservices Architecture
modules.intro: Microservices interviews are the broadest backend topic — the module has the most topics because the surface is huge. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with fundamentals (what microservices are, why, the trade-offs), then service design (decomposition by business capability). The communication tier follows — API gateway, service discovery, load balancing, the patterns that make services find and talk to each other. Resilience (circuit breaker, saga) is the production tier, then observability (distributed tracing) and verification (contract testing). Feign, migration strategies, and service mesh close out the advanced tier. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Messaging & Event-Driven Architecture
modules.intro: Messaging and events is the asynchronous-systems interview surface. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with messaging fundamentals (queues vs topics, delivery semantics), then Kafka architecture (the partition, the broker, the consumer group — the centerpiece). Message guarantees (at-least-once, exactly-once) and Kafka patterns follow, then Spring Kafka (the code tier). Webhooks sit alongside as the HTTP-event model. The advanced tier covers event sourcing, CQRS, and stream processing. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: RabbitMQ & AMQP
modules.intro: RabbitMQ is a single-topic module. This module covers RabbitMQ fundamentals — exchanges, queues, bindings, the AMQP model, durability, acknowledgements, dead-letter queues — organized as an elevation arc within the one topic from 'what is RabbitMQ' through to production reliability patterns.

modules.title: Design Patterns & SOLID
modules.intro: Design-pattern interviews test whether you can apply a pattern to a real problem, not just name it. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with SOLID (the design-principle foundation), then the three GoF categories — creational, structural, behavioral — in order of how often they're asked. From there it moves to refactoring and technical debt (the applied tier: when patterns meet legacy code), then the legacy-patterns and comparison canon. It closes with scenario-based questions where you choose the right pattern for a stated problem.

modules.title: Architecture Patterns & Principles
modules.intro: Architecture-pattern interviews test whether you can choose a structure and defend it. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with architectural styles (the landscape — monolith, layered, microservices, event-driven), then the two most-asked patterns — clean architecture and hexagonal (ports & adapters) — then domain-driven design (the strategic patterns: bounded contexts, aggregates). Microservices patterns follow at the applied tier, then the comparison canon, then scenario-based design questions. It closes with CQRS and event sourcing — the advanced patterns that separate architects from developers.

modules.title: System Design Fundamentals
modules.intro: System design interviews are the senior/staff round that tests whether you can architect at scale. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with design fundamentals (the approach, the requirements gathering), then the core primitives — scalability, load balancing, caching, the CAP theorem. High availability and database design at scale follow, then the architecture patterns — event-driven and microservices design. Capacity planning closes the advanced tier, then comparisons and scenario-based design questions.

modules.title: System Design Case Studies
modules.intro: System design cases are the concrete interview problems that apply the system-design primitives. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with URL shortener (the classic warm-up), then rate limiter, then the communication systems (chat, notification) that test real-time design. Search autocomplete and social media feed are the scale tier, then payment system — the hardest because it adds idempotency and consistency. It closes with scenario-based variants.

modules.title: Application Security & OWASP
modules.intro: Application security interviews test whether you can reason about threats, not just recite acronyms. This module opens with security architecture (the defense-in-depth model), then the OWASP Top 10 — the canonical vulnerability list every interviewer references. From there it builds outward: encryption (the math you must get right), secrets management (where keys actually live), secure coding (the patterns that prevent the OWASP issues), then verification — vulnerability scanning and security testing. It closes with compliance, the comparison canon, and scenario-based questions where the threats meet real code.

modules.title: Java Testing
modules.intro: Testing interviews test whether you understand testing as a strategy, not just whether you write tests. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with unit-testing basics and TDD (the foundation), then Mockito (the mocking tool every Java test uses). Integration testing and Spring Boot testing are the framework tier, then Testcontainers (the modern integration approach). Testing strategies, automation, and contract testing follow, then the specialized tiers — performance, chaos. Unit-testing advanced closes the depth tier, then comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Git
modules.intro: Git interviews test whether you understand the model, not just the commands. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with Git internals (the DAG, objects, branches as pointers — the model that makes everything else make sense), then workflows (GitFlow, trunk-based), then code-quality gates (hooks, pre-commit). It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Maven & Gradle (Java Build Tools)
modules.intro: Build-tool interviews test whether you understand the build lifecycle, not just run the commands. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with Maven (the dominant Java build tool — the lifecycle, POM, dependency resolution), then Gradle (the modern alternative — the task graph, Kotlin DSL). It closes with the Maven-vs-Gradle comparison canon and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: CI/CD Pipelines
modules.intro: CI/CD interviews test whether you understand the pipeline as a system, not a script. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with CI/CD fundamentals (the build-test-deploy loop, why it exists), then GitHub Actions (the most-asked modern CI tool), then deployment strategies (blue-green, canary, rolling), then rollback strategies (the thing that saves you at 2am). It closes with comparisons and scenario-based pipeline-design questions.

modules.title: Terraform & Infrastructure-as-Code
modules.intro: Terraform is a single-topic module. This module covers Terraform core — HCL, resources, state, modules, workspaces, variables, backend, the plan/apply lifecycle — organized as an elevation arc within the one topic from 'what is Terraform and IaC' through to production patterns (state locking, module design, drift).

modules.title: Jenkins CI
modules.intro: Jenkins is a single-topic module. This module covers Jenkins pipelines — declarative vs scripted, Jenkinsfiles, shared libraries, agents, parallel stages — organized as an elevation arc within the one topic from 'what is a Jenkins pipeline' through to production CI/CD patterns.

modules.title: Docker & Containerization
modules.intro: Docker interviews test whether you understand containers as an isolation primitive, not just a build command. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with Docker fundamentals (image vs container, the engine), then multi-stage builds (the production pattern for small images). Compose, networking, and security follow at the applied tier. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Kubernetes & Orchestration
modules.intro: Kubernetes interviews test whether you understand the declarative model, not just kubectl. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with Kubernetes fundamentals (the control plane, pods, the reconcilation loop), then workloads (Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs), then networking (Services, Ingress, CNI) and configuration (ConfigMaps, Secrets). Helm follows at the applied tier, then scaling (HPA, VPA, cluster autoscaler). It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: AWS, Cloud & Cloud-Native Architecture
modules.intro: AWS interviews test whether you can pick the right managed service and wire it to a Spring app. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with the core services (EC2, VPC, the primitives), then containers (ECS/Fargate — the modern deploy unit), then S3, IAM, and RDS (the services every backend touches). Messaging (SNS/SQS/Kinesis) and serverless (Lambda) follow at the applied tier, then the comparison canon and scenario-based architecture questions.

modules.title: Cloud-Native & Cloud Architecture
modules.intro: Cloud-native interviews test whether you design for the cloud's failure model, not just deploy to it. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with the 12-factor app (the canonical cloud-native methodology), then cloud design patterns (circuit breaker, sidecar, ambassador), then deployment strategies. Comparisons and scenarios follow, then the advanced tier — cost optimization, multi-region architecture, and disaster recovery — the concerns that separate a cloud-native architect from someone who just uses managed services.

modules.title: Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
modules.intro: GCP interviews mirror the other clouds but with Google's product names. This module is an elevation arc: core services first (Compute Engine, VPC), then compute and deployment (GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Functions), storage and data (GCS, Cloud SQL, Spanner), messaging (Pub/Sub), security and IAM, and observability (Cloud Monitoring, Logging).

modules.title: Microsoft Azure
modules.intro: Azure interviews mirror AWS but with Microsoft's naming and portal. This module is an elevation arc: core services first (the primitives), then compute and deployment (App Service, AKS, Functions), then storage and data (Cosmos DB, Blob), messaging (Service Bus, Event Grid), security and IAM (Entra ID), and observability (Application Insights, Monitor).

modules.title: Observability & Monitoring
modules.intro: Observability interviews test whether you can debug a distributed system you can't see into. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with the three pillars — structured logging, metrics (Micrometer), and distributed tracing — then the visualization layer (Prometheus and Grafana). Health checks and alerting are the production tier, then APM tools and log aggregation. It closes with comparisons and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Production Operations & SRE
modules.intro: Production and SRE interviews test whether you've shipped and survived — the operational maturity round. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with SRE practices (the discipline — SLIs/SLOs, error budgets), then the incident lifecycle (management, response, on-call). Debugging production and performance troubleshooting are the core-mechanics tier, then root-cause analysis and postmortems (the learning loop). Runbooks, capacity planning, and the deep-debugging tier (memory leaks, thread/heap dumps) follow, with chaos engineering at the advanced tier. It closes with scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Behavioral, Leadership & Engineering Practices
modules.intro: Behavioral interviews are graded on structure, not answers. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with the STAR method (the framework every behavioral answer should use), then the pressure questions (delivering under pressure, failure and learning — the 'tell me about a time' canon), then interpersonal (conflict resolution), then forward-looking (career growth). It closes with agile and scrum — the process questions that round out a behavioral round.

modules.title: Engineering Practices & Technical Leadership
modules.intro: Engineering-practices interviews (often the staff/senior round) test how you operate, not just what you build. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with code review (the daily practice), then architecture decisions (ADRs — how you record trade-offs), then technical debt (how you manage it without going bankrupt). From there it moves to leadership, mentoring, knowledge sharing, and documentation — the multiplier practices. It closes with team collaboration and scenario-based questions.

modules.title: Low-Level Design (LLD)
modules.intro: Low-level design (LLD) interviews test whether you can model a real system in classes. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with LLD fundamentals (identating classes, SOLID in design, the approach), then the classic interview problems in order of difficulty — parking lot, elevator system, vending machine, and splitwise. Each problem builds on the patterns of the previous one.

modules.title: AI & LLM Integration for Java
modules.intro: LLM-powered Spring applications are the newest backend interview surface. This module is an elevation arc: it opens with what Spring AI is and how it fits the Spring ecosystem, then prompt engineering (the lever you control), then wiring LLM APIs into a Spring app (rate limits, retries, function calling). From there it moves to RAG — the architecture most production LLM features use — and the vector databases that back it. It closes with the two tiers that separate shipped from demo: testing LLM features (evaluation, mocking) and observing them in production (cost, metrics, tracing).
